title: Credit Analysis Basics for Beginners: A Practical Guide
excerpt: Learn a beginner-friendly credit analysis workflow for understanding business, financial statements, cash flow, repayment capacity, risks and evidence.

body.text: Credit analysis is a structured review of information relevant to a proposed or existing credit exposure. A beginner can learn to organize evidence, understand financial statements, examine cash generation and identify questions that need an authorized reviewer. Credit analysis is not simply a ratio calculation and does not by itself approve a loan. Lenders use their own policies, data, decision rights and applicable requirements. This guide provides an educational workflow and a fictional example; it does not assess a real borrower, recommend a lending decision or claim a separate credit-analysis course at Centaur Careers.
Define the question before opening the spreadsheet

Start by identifying the purpose of the analysis: a new application, periodic review, limit change, portfolio monitoring or an information request. These tasks may need different periods, evidence and approvals. Confirm the borrower or counterparty identity through the approved process and record what entity is being assessed. Then identify the facility or exposure, proposed amount, term and repayment source if these are within the analyst's assigned scope. Do not assume that every file contains the same fields or that a template replaces the institution's policy. A clear scope prevents a learner from producing calculations that answer the wrong question.

items: Who is the borrower and what is the legal or operating entity under review?
What is the purpose, amount, term and stated repayment source of the request?
Which period and financial statements are available, and who prepared them?
What information is missing, stale, inconsistent or still unverified?
Who is authorized to decide, review, request information or approve an exception?

body.text: Understand the business and its cash cycle

Before ratios, understand how the business earns and uses cash. Identify its products or services, customers, suppliers, seasonality, major operating costs, working-capital cycle and dependence on a small number of counterparties. Ask what could disrupt revenue or collections and whether the company has practical alternatives. A bank or analyst may require different evidence depending on the sector and facility. For a small wholesaler, inventory and receivables may be central; for a project business, milestones and completion timing may matter. These are prompts, not a complete industry checklist.

Then connect the business narrative to the statements. Revenue should be compared with receivables and collection patterns; margins should be viewed with cost and volume changes; debt should be compared with the entity's ability to service it; and cash movement should be reconciled with the operating cycle. If the story and figures do not agree, identify the gap and request evidence through the approved channel. Avoid treating management projections as actual results or assuming that historical performance will repeat.
Read the statements as a connected set

The income statement summarizes performance over a period, the balance sheet presents resources and obligations at a point in time, and the cash-flow statement explains cash movements under its reporting framework. They should be read together. Profit does not automatically mean cash is available to repay debt. A rise in receivables or inventory may consume cash; capital expenditure can reduce free cash; and a change in borrowing may temporarily improve liquidity while increasing future obligations. Confirm the statement dates, accounting basis, audit or review status and whether figures are standalone or consolidated before comparing them.

items: Check that statement periods are comparable and the reporting currency and units are consistent.
Trace major totals to notes, schedules or source documents where available and authorized.
Notice differences between profit, operating cash and closing cash rather than treating them as synonyms.
Review debt maturity and repayment obligations against forecast cash generation.
Flag related-party, one-off or unusual items for qualified review instead of making unsupported adjustments.

body.text: Use ratios as questions, not verdicts

Liquidity, leverage, coverage, profitability and efficiency ratios can help organize analysis, but definitions vary and no single threshold is universally safe. A current ratio compares selected current assets and liabilities; a debt-to-equity measure compares defined debt with an equity base; interest coverage compares an earnings measure with interest expense. The exact numerator and denominator should be stated. Ratios can be distorted by seasonality, accounting policies, one-off items, sector economics or inconsistent classification. Compare trends, peer context where reliable, and the underlying amounts. A ratio suggests a question; it does not make the decision.
Fictional example: distinguish profit from repayment capacity

Consider a fictional distributor that reports a year-on-year increase in profit but also a large increase in receivables and inventory. The income statement appears stronger, yet collections have lengthened and inventory turnover slowed. Before concluding that repayment capacity improved, an analyst would examine aging, customer concentration, stock quality, supplier terms and the timing of cash flows. If the company's forecast assumes every late invoice is collected next month, that assumption needs evidence and a downside scenario. This example is invented and intentionally contains no credit recommendation or real company data.

A concise analytical note might say: 'Reported profit increased in the period; operating cash did not improve by the same amount. Receivables and inventory require further support. The next review should reconcile the largest movements to source schedules and test a lower-collection scenario.' That wording distinguishes fact from interpretation and specifies what remains open. A weak note would label the borrower safe or risky without explaining what data supports that conclusion or which decision-maker has authority.
Document uncertainty and escalation

A professional analysis records source, date, author, definition, assumption and unresolved item. It states when information is unaudited, management-prepared, estimated or missing. If a value conflicts between documents, preserve the source records and ask for clarification rather than editing the number silently. If a potential covenant, fraud, privacy or regulatory issue appears, follow the institution's escalation procedure. Analysts should avoid requesting more personal or sensitive data than authorized and should handle documents in approved systems. The reviewer should be able to reproduce key calculations and understand why a question was raised.

items: Summarize the entity and purpose of review in neutral terms.
List evidence reviewed and date each source was obtained.
Show key calculations with formulas, units and stated definitions.
Separate verified facts, management assertions, analyst assumptions and open questions.
Route the note to the authorized credit reviewer; do not imply approval or promise an outcome.

body.text: Practise the workflow as a beginner

Use a synthetic company dataset to practise linking statement lines, calculating a few clearly defined ratios, tracking cash movements and writing a one-page note. Add an intentionally missing document and one inconsistent reporting date to test how you flag data-quality issues. Do not use another person's credit report, confidential employer file or real customer details. In a portfolio, label the project as fictional, describe what you did not evaluate, and avoid showing a credit score or a yes/no approval. That is safer and more credible than presenting a classroom worksheet as a lender's decision model.
Turn a credit review into a traceable workpaper

A good beginner workpaper starts with a short question and a contents list. State the borrower or fictional entity, purpose of review, reporting period and status of each source. Put raw inputs in one area and calculations in another so a reviewer can distinguish source facts from analyst transformations. Define every ratio, display units, identify missing records and show a second check for the most important formula. If one statement is unaudited or covers a different period, label it near the figure rather than burying the caveat in a footnote.

The narrative can follow a consistent order: business model, recent performance, balance-sheet position, cash generation, debt and repayment, risks, mitigants, unanswered questions and next action. This is not an approval format. It is a way to help an authorized person find evidence and challenge assumptions. The analyst should avoid copying a standard paragraph that says a business is 'stable' without explaining what data supports that view. A short, specific note is more useful than a long list of ratios with no interpretation.

If a reviewer disagrees with an assumption, the workpaper should make revision possible. Keep formulas visible, record the new assumption and date, and preserve the previous version according to the learning exercise's controls. In a real institution, versioning and retention follow policy. A correction should not erase the fact that a discrepancy existed or who approved the change. This approach builds the habit of treating analytical work as a reviewable record rather than a personal opinion.

items: Source register with document date, period, currency and reliability status.
Formula register with numerator, denominator and units for each ratio.
Assumption log with owner, rationale, sensitivity and open validation.
Exception list with evidence needed, due date and reviewer.
Conclusion limited to the analyst's assigned role and authority.

body.text: Frequently asked questions

body.question: What is credit analysis in simple terms?
body.answer: It is a structured review of information relevant to a credit exposure, including business context, financial evidence, cash generation, obligations, risks and unanswered questions. The authorized lender makes decisions under its policy.

body.question: Which financial statement matters most in credit analysis?
body.answer: No one statement is sufficient in every case. Performance, financial position and cash flows provide connected information; the relevant evidence depends on the borrower, product and purpose of review.

body.question: Do credit ratios decide whether a loan is approved?
body.answer: No. Ratios are analytical indicators whose definitions and interpretation depend on context. An authorized decision process considers multiple forms of evidence and applicable policy.

body.question: Can I practise credit analysis with public company data?
body.answer: You can use lawfully available public information for an educational exercise, cite sources, state the reporting date and limitations, and avoid presenting the exercise as a real lender decision.
